extracted.intended_audience: students of journalism and young reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive textbook guidance on gathering, evaluating, structuring, and styling news stories, with examples and methods for analysis aimed at journalism students and beginning reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The news which the story contains should be typical, rather than extraordinary or 'freakish'; and the story should present the news effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specimens chosen for study ought to show average practice so students learn to handle common reporting tasks first; examples may include less-perfect work to show what to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fiction methods with strict truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of the methods of fiction in portraying actual events is commendable; substituting fictitious details to heighten effect is forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No stories unquestionably fictitious are included; some with imaginary details are provided only to furnish material for discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A story is most effective when its structure and style enable the reader to get the news with the least effort and the greatest interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because newspapers are read rapidly, prioritize clarity, concise summary leads, and placing essential facts where they catch the eye quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: News writing must be concise — needless words omitted, only necessary details given, and story length proportionate to importance of material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mantras in the office: 'Boil it down' and 'Cut it to the bone.' Conciseness need not be bald or unattractive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness (simplicity of diction and construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearness is secured by comparative simplicity of diction, sentence construction, and paragraph structure; learned diction, elaborate figures, and involved sentences have no place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt style to be easily grasped by rapid readers of varied education levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: The style of writing is generally adapted to readers of limited education no less than to the well educated; comparative simplicity of expression is the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider character of readers and present material to interest both 'masses' and professional classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis by initial position
rubrics_metrics.description: Important details are placed at the beginning of paragraphs and sentences where they will catch the eye at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields loose rather than periodic sentence structure and reduces climactic effects; use initial position to give prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical constraints and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The typographical form (narrow columns, short lines) determines paragraph and sentence length and affects style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspaper paragraphs should be shorter (typical 35–75 words); line-shortness (about six words per line) requires briefer paragraphs than book prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to reading conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: News must be written for rapid reading: easy to read, attractive in form and style, and suited to the way newspapers are consumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use devices (frames/boxes, bold-face) to highlight facts; consider how reading conditions influence structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of newspaper contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversified newspaper contents may be grouped in seven classes: (1) news stories; (2) special feature articles; (3) editorials; (4) dramatic, musical and literary criticism; (5) practical advice and useful information; (6) humorous matter; (7) fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of these, the first four are the distinctly journalistic types; know distinctions when choosing form and treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of news stories (informative vs feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two general types: (1) the informative news story—chief aim to give the facts; (2) the feature or human interest story—chief aim to make material of little/no news value interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informative stories may be purely informative or constructive (aim to produce wholesome effect); feature stories test literary ability and depend on sustaining reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informative story subtypes (pure vs constructive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informative stories: (1) record facts without regard to effect; (2) present facts to produce a wholesome/constructive effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive stories may emphasize causes, responsibility, frequency to prompt preventive measures and civic improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story methods (discourse forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories in method are narrative, descriptive, expository, or combinations of these forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative informative stories usually have little suspense because essentials are summarized in the lead; narrative features may sustain suspense using fiction devices; description may be suggestive or detailed depending on space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: beginning (lead) and body
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of the news story concerns (1) the beginning, or lead, and (2) the body of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The informative story usually begins with a summary lead that answers Who? What? Where? When? Why? How? The body follows a logical order (often chronological), repeats only necessary lead details, and rounds out the story but endings may be truncated by make-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary lead elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A summary lead includes: (1) the persons, (2) the event, (3) the place, (4) the time, (5) the cause, (6) the significant circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any one of these elements may be 'featured' in the place of prominence at the beginning; feature stories often avoid the summary lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and ethical duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Every news story should present details as accurately and completely as the significance warrants; embellishment with fictitious details, distortion, and suppression of significant facts are opposed to the fundamental purpose of the newspaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond accuracy, writers should be aware that presentation affects readers and may be constructive or destructive; avoid making wrongdoing attractive or glamorizing crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values (what counts as news)
rubrics_metrics.description: News is anything timely that interests a number of readers; the best news has the greatest interest for the greatest number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values include: timely matters; extraordinary events/circumstances; struggles for supremacy (politics, business, sports); matters involving property, life, welfare of people; children; animals; hobbies/amusements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of reader interest factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of reader interest is proportionate to (1) familiarity with persons/places/things involved, (2) importance/prominence of those persons/places/things, (3) closeness of their relation to the reader's personal affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local interest often outweighs distant events; bring out 'local ends' of general news to increase relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation indicated by space/placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each story indicates the evaluation of its news by reporter/editor; the importance as judged is shown by the space given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should examine why space was allocated and use that as a criterion for their own news judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of news
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sources include public and private records, reports, officials, eye-witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note sources carefully; compile lists of sources for different kinds of stories (crime, fires, accidents) to draw upon in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of news gathering
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how details were obtained — interviews, observation, records, correspondence; the story often shows circumstances under which material was secured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer reporters' questions from replies; note hints about circumstances; telephone, mail, telegraph, or rewrite men may be used depending on urgency and distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: News gathering organization (local vs telegraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: News is divided into local news (gathered by reporters under city editor or news bureau) and telegraph news (non-local, sent by telegraph, telephone, cable, or mail).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the different editorial lines and responsibilities (press association correspondents responsible to association division heads; newspaper correspondents to telegraph or state editor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis checklist for studying stories
rubrics_metrics.description: In studying a news story consider: (1) value of the news; (2) sources of the news; (3) methods by which it was obtained; (4) purpose of the story; (5) type of the story; (6) structure; (7) literary style; (8) typographical style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist to discover how to obtain, evaluate, and present news most effectively; compare multiple examples of same type to see variety of treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary style qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Style concerns paragraphs, sentences, words and qualities like clearness, force, animation, humor, pathos, taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze paragraph/sentence length, unity of thought/topic, coherence, and emphasis by position; avoid long periodic sentences and involved constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical stance on sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical view of newspapers that give prominence to sensational, ghastly, and scandalous phases of news for morbid appeal; this is contrasted with constructive treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive newspapers emphasize causes, responsibilities and preventive measures; sensationalism may have unwholesome effects and should be resisted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation and innovation in form
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular demand for novelty and variety prevents fixed forms and produces new forms/styles; some papers abandon conventional summary beginnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when unconventional leads or narrative devices are appropriate to make stories entertaining, but retain accuracy and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and collaborative authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all stories as printed are the work of reporter(s) and one or more editors and copy-readers; well-written stories undergo little change, poor stories may be remade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that rewrite men and editors shape final copy; learn to write copy that needs minimal reworking.
